skills.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray for tracheal abnormalities and associated parenchymal lung disease, specifically to distinguish between well-defined nodular opacities and ill-defined infiltrates.
steps: Inspect the tracheal caliber on the frontal view; confirm tracheomegaly if the transverse diameter significantly exceeds normal limits (e.g., >25 mm in men, >21 mm in women) or appears markedly widened relative to the thoracic inlet.
Systematically scan the lung fields to locate opacities, paying attention to their margins and distribution.

Differentiate 'well-defined' from 'ill-defined' opacities: Well-defined opacities have sharp, distinct borders suggesting nodules, masses, or cysts (often seen in bronchiectasis or specific infections), whereas ill-defined opacities have hazy, fuzzy borders suggesting alveolar filling, edema, or active inflammation.
Verify the laterality (left vs. right) and vertical zone (upper, middle, lower) of the identified findings to ensure accurate anatomical localization.

skills.trigger: When describing the specific anatomical distribution of pulmonary findings on a chest radiograph to differentiate between similar diagnostic options.
steps: Identify the primary airway abnormality (e.g., tracheal widening) as the anchor point for the syndrome.
Divide the lungs into zones (upper, mid, lower) and sides (left, right) using anatomical landmarks like ribs and fissures.
Characterize the texture of opacities in each zone: look for discrete, rounded densities (nodular/well-defined) versus reticular, linear, or hazy patterns.

Correlate the side and zone of the nodular/well-defined opacities with the side and zone of the linear/reticular opacities to form a complete spatial description (e.g., 'right lower lobe nodules' vs 'left base linear opacities').
